title: A follower that takes the commit index on the heartbeat after an entry, proved live
summary: A Raft follower that appends an entry takes the leader's commit index in the same request, as far as the entries it now holds. A developer has it take the commit index only on a request that appends nothing, the heartbeat that follows, once the entry is on disk: a request that appends is a write, and the commit index moves on the next one. The change is verified under all three configurations, the two safety ones in 21,551 and 9,269 states, and the fairness one in 14,958: every entry still reaches every follower, every follower still learns the leader's commits, a leader's own entries are still committed, and the coverage shows both rows the change alters taken under each.

change.description: In `AppendRule.decide`, the `ABSENT` and `CONFLICTING` arms for the entry sent no longer add `ADVANCE_COMMIT` when the leader's commit index is ahead: they return `transition(MATCHING, APPEND)` and `transition(MATCHING, TRUNCATE, APPEND)` whatever the commit index, with the comment that the commit index moves on the next heartbeat, once the entry is on disk. The `NONE, SAME` arm still takes it. The Javadoc says the commit index follows the leader's on a request that carries no entry, and the test of the commit index splits into one for the heartbeat and one that an entry is appended before its commit is taken.

risk: Low, and the question a reviewer asks is the one example 099 answers in the negative: whether a follower that takes the commit index later takes it at all. Here the rows that take it are the heartbeat's, which the leader sends as long as it leads, and the rows that no longer take it are followed by a heartbeat as soon as the follower is caught up. The safety configurations cannot tell this change from 099, since both move the commit index later; the fairness one can.
explanation: The append rule in the model is generated from the regenerated contract, so `Replicate` does what the two patched rows say, the two of the four edited whose decision changes: a request that appends leaves the follower's commit index where it was, and the heartbeat after it, with nothing to append and the leader's commit index ahead, moves it. TLC verifies the change under all three configurations: 21,551 states of three terms and two entries, 9,269 of figure 8, and 14,958 of the fairness configuration, under which every follower's log comes to hold the leader's, every follower's commit index comes to be no less than the leader's, and every entry a leader appends in its term is committed unless the leader is deposed. The coverage shows both rows the change alters taken by a step of the model under each configuration, so the verdict rests on runs in which a follower appends an entry the leader has already committed and takes the commit index on the request after. What the fairness condition on `Replicate` provides is the heartbeat: a leader that sends every follower its next entry or a heartbeat as long as it leads is the assumption under which postponing the commit index by one request costs nothing but the request. Under the fourth configuration, two terms and one entry per leader with replies delayed, TLC verifies the change in 267,588 states, with both changed rows taken there as well.
resolution: Merge. Taking the commit index on the heartbeat after an entry rather than with it is a reordering the protocol allows, since the commit index is carried by every request and a follower applies the leader's as far as its log matches; what the change costs is a round trip of staleness on a follower, which the fairness configuration shows to be a round trip and not forever, where example 099's change, which also postpones the commit index, postpones it for good. The rows are checked under all three configurations on every build, and the liveness properties are what distinguish the two changes.
notes: The Raft replication model (`apps/quorum/spec/RaftReplication.tla`) has the logs live, around the follower's append rule and the leader's commit rule as generated operators beside the role machine and the vote rule, and checks log matching, leader completeness and state machine safety, with an action property that no committed entry is ever overwritten. Its configurations are three terms with two entries, and the four terms of the paper's figure 8.

`RaftReplicationLive.cfg` checks three temporal properties for runs within the term budget: every entry in a leader's log reaches every follower, every follower learns the leader's commits, and an entry a leader appends in its term is committed unless the leader is deposed.
Taking the commit index only on the heartbeat after an entry is proved safe and live under all three configurations.
provenance: Constructed as the third example of the replication model's liveness configuration, to pair with 099 and 100: a change to the rows next to 099's, correct this time, which the safety configurations cannot tell apart from 099 and the fairness one accepts.

references.title: Ongaro and Ousterhout, In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (extended version, 2014): section 5.3, log replication, the consistency check and the commit index in AppendEntries; section 8, the no-op entry a leader commits at the start of its term

Ongaro, the TLA+ specification of Raft (raft.tla): HandleAppendEntriesRequest, which takes the leader's commit index on every accepted request, and AdvanceCommitIndex over every index a majority agrees on
Lamport, Specifying Systems (2002): chapter 8, liveness and fairness; weak fairness WF_v(A) and the leads-to operator

TLC's liveness checking: a temporal property's counterexample is a run that goes on forever, a prefix then a state (Stuttering) or a cycle (Back to state N) the system never leaves; unsound under a symmetry set
